_meta.purpose: The FINOS AI Governance Framework in CatalogFile shape, so applyCatalogFile creates the framework, its 25 requirements (one per mitigation), one control template per requirement, their requirement links and the pack together.
_meta.grounding: Requirement codes, titles, sections and summaries are generated from src/data/libraries/finos-aigf.yaml, so the library import and this catalogue write identical requirement rows. Every template, title through tasks, is authored in this repo from what each mitigation asks an organisation to demonstrate.
_meta.grain: One template per mitigation. FINOS writes each mitigation as a self-contained control with its own owner and evidence, so it is the unit a tenant implements and the unit it can mark not applicable.
_meta.cadence: FINOS sets no evidence cadence, so every template is ANNUALLY, the catalogue default. A tighter cadence would be an Inflect judgement presented as FINOS's.
_meta.licensing: FINOS AIGF is CC-BY-4.0. Only mitigation identifiers and short titles are FINOS's; all prose is Inflect's. Attribution in framework.metadata.copyright.
_meta.frameworkKeyNote: Deliberately the SAME key as src/data/libraries/finos-aigf.yaml, so the library import and this fixture converge on ONE Framework row. No edition in the key: the AIGF is revised in place.

framework.name: FINOS AI Governance Framework
framework.description: The FINOS AI Governance Framework (AIGF) is an open catalogue of the risks of running AI systems in financial services, and of the mitigations that address them, maintained by the Fintech Open Source Foundation. Inflect carries each mitigation as one requirement, with FINOS identifiers and short titles and Inflect-written descriptions of what the mitigation asks an organisation to demonstrate. The risks are in the risk-template library.

requirements.title: Data Filtering From External Knowledge Bases
requirements.summary: An organisation should be able to show that content taken from its internal knowledge sources (wikis, document stores, databases and collaboration sites) is cleaned before it is embedded, indexed or sent to a model: sensitive categories are identified, each has a set treatment such as masking, redaction or tokenisation, the pipeline applies and records those treatments, material too sensitive to clean sits in a separate AI environment, and sampling shows what the filters missed.

requirements.title: User/App/Model Firewalling/Filtering
requirements.summary: The organisation can show that every point where data passes into or out of a model has a written set of checks: prompts from users, responses back to them, calls between application components, and internal content sent to an outside service to be turned into embeddings. It can show which checks are static patterns and which rely on a classifier or judge model, how streamed replies are handled, that every check logs what it blocks or alters, and that the checks are tested against attack and leakage samples. Running a dedicated firewall product is a separate matter, covered by MI-17.

requirements.title: System Acceptance Testing
requirements.summary: An organisation must be able to show that before an AI system goes live it was tested against acceptance criteria agreed in advance with the business and control functions, in an environment and with data representative of production, with real users taking part; that because model output varies, the criteria assert required or forbidden content and an accepted pass rate rather than exact wording; that defects were tracked and the serious ones re-tested; and that the business owner signed the release with known limitations stated. Ongoing evaluation after release belongs to MI-15.

requirements.title: Data Quality & Classification/Sensitivity
requirements.summary: An organisation should be able to show that every source of data used to train, test or run its AI systems is documented with its purpose, limits and lineage, carries a sensitivity label from the organisation's own classification scheme, and is measured against quality dimensions and thresholds the organisation has set; and that pipelines hold back data that fails those thresholds or exceeds its permitted sensitivity until someone fixes or authorises it.

requirements.title: Legal and Contractual Frameworks for AI Systems
requirements.summary: An organisation must be able to show that every external party supplying an AI model, inference service, training data or AI tooling is bound by a written agreement, and that the organisation understands what that agreement commits each side to. The agreement settles what the supplier does with prompts, outputs and other data sent to it, how intellectual property in training data and outputs is treated, who carries which lifecycle duty and liability, the service levels, and how the supplier announces model changes. Terms are checked against internal requirements before signature and revisited as usage changes.

requirements.title: Quality of Service (QoS) and DDoS Prevention for AI Systems
requirements.summary: The organisation can show that its AI services stay usable for legitimate users when traffic is heavy or hostile. That means per-key or per-user request limits, throttling of bursts, validation that turns away malformed or very costly requests, network-level flood protection, load balancing with failover, isolation of core inference from overloaded upstream parts, priority for critical work when capacity runs short, and monitoring that catches abusive traffic early. Budget and spend alerting is MI-9's subject, and content filtering of prompts is MI-3's.

requirements.title: AI Model Version Pinning
requirements.summary: The organisation can show that each production AI system calls a specific, approved model version rather than whatever the provider currently serves, and that moving to a new version is a deliberate, tested and reversible change. It can show an inventory of deployed models and their pinned versions, supplier commitments on versioning, release notes and deprecation notice, a record of which version produced each output, an evaluation of each candidate version against the current baseline, staged rollout with a working rollback, and periodic checks that production matches the approved versions. Acceptance testing in full is MI-5's subject.

requirements.title: Role-Based Access Control for AI Data
requirements.summary: An organisation should be able to show who and what may read, change or delete the data its AI systems are built and run on: a defined set of human roles and non-human identities such as models, pipelines and service accounts, a matrix tying each to data classes and actions on least privilege with conflicting duties separated, enforcement at every store, platform, API and application, strong authentication, logged access, and periodic recertification by data owners.

requirements.title: Encryption of AI Data at Rest
requirements.summary: An organisation should be able to show that everything its AI systems store persistently is encrypted: training and test sets, intermediate artefacts, embeddings in vector databases, model files, logs, configuration and every backup. It should hold an encryption standard matched to its classification scheme, keys managed in a dedicated key management system with restricted access and rotation, evidence that hosted and self-run vector stores have encryption actually switched on, and periodic checks that it remains so.

requirements.title: AI Firewall Implementation and Management
requirements.summary: The organisation can show that a dedicated AI firewall layer, whether a gateway, a security proxy, an extended web application firewall or a guardian model, is deployed against a written policy of what it must stop. It can show where the layer sits in each AI traffic path, the latency it adds, how its rules and threat signatures are kept current, that its alerts reach the security monitoring and response tooling, and that it is tested for bypass, missed threats and false blocks. The filtering rules themselves are MI-3's subject and the scoping of agent permissions is MI-18's.

requirements.title: Agent Authority Least Privilege Framework
requirements.summary: The organisation can show, for every agent it runs, a written list of the tools, APIs, endpoints and data sources that agent is allowed to use, each grant justified by the agent's job. It can show that a component the agent cannot alter refuses and logs any call outside that list, including commands run at the operating-system level, that any temporary widening was approved by a person and lapsed afterwards, and that grants nobody uses are taken away. Isolation between agents, credential handling and the approval mechanism itself are separate mitigations.

requirements.title: Tool Chain Validation and Sanitization
requirements.summary: An organisation running agents that choose and call tools must be able to show that each call is checked at the moment it runs: that the tool chosen suits the task and the caller's authority, that every parameter passed to an API meets its expected type, format, range and business rules and cannot carry an injection, that data handed from one tool to the next is cleaned before reuse, and that the order of calls follows an approved pattern. Validation failures reach security monitoring, and the rules themselves are version controlled, tested and kept current.

requirements.title: MCP Server Security Governance
requirements.summary: An organisation whose agents use MCP servers must be able to show that it decides which servers may be connected, vets each one before approval, and enforces that decision technically so clients cannot reach unapproved servers. It records the implementation it approved and the level of protection it chose for its deployment, protects the connection with encryption and authentication, watches server behaviour and security advisories, can cut off a compromised server quickly, and re-reviews approved servers over time.

requirements.title: Multi-Agent Isolation and Segmentation
requirements.summary: Where several agents work together, the organisation can show that each runs in its own compartment, with its own runtime account, state, memory, cache and temporary storage, and that agents talk to each other only over authenticated channels along routes a written matrix allows. It can show the trust levels it assigned to agents and why, that a failing or compromised agent can be cut off without bringing down the rest, and that the boundaries have been tested. What each agent may do on its own is covered by least privilege, and its secrets by credential protection.

requirements.title: Agentic System Credential Protection Framework
requirements.summary: The organisation can show that its agents run without stored secrets in their images, environment variables or file systems, that they receive only short-lived credentials scoped to the task through a broker that checks who is asking, and that secret stores, credential administration interfaces and credential-revealing tools are out of their reach. It can also show that it watches agent behaviour for signs of credential hunting and that it can rotate and revoke exposed credentials quickly. What an agent may do with the access it holds is a separate least-privilege matter.

requirements.title: Human-in-the-Loop Action Approval Gate
requirements.summary: The organisation can show which agent actions it has designated as needing a person's approval and why, and that each such action is held before any side effect until an authorised approver, never the requester or the agent, decides on the exact resolved action through a channel that cannot be spoofed or replayed. It can show the record linking action, rule, approver and outcome, how standing pre-approvals are bounded and attributed, and that tests could not push a gated action through without approval. What the agent may reach at all is set by least privilege. FINOS publishes this mitigation as a draft.

requirements.title: Skill/Plugin Integrity and Governance
requirements.summary: An organisation that lets agents load skills or plugins, bundles of instructions and often scripts that run with the agent's authority, must be able to show that only reviewed versions load. It knows which skills are installed and where they came from, reviews both instruction text and bundled code and dependencies before approval, distributes approved versions from a controlled source, verifies at load time that a skill matches what was approved, re-reviews changes, and detects attempts to load anything else. FINOS publishes this mitigation as a draft.

requirements.title: AI Data Leakage Prevention and Detection
requirements.summary: An organisation should be able to show that it knows every route by which conversation data, proprietary training sets and model weights could leave its control through an AI system, including calls to externally hosted model providers; that each route carries preventive safeguards proportionate to the harm a leak would cause; and that planted markers, data fingerprints and monitoring would reveal a leak that got past those safeguards and send it into incident handling.

requirements.title: AI System Observability
requirements.summary: An organisation must be able to show that each AI system it runs emits structured logs, metrics and traces covering what users sent, what the model returned, the calls made to models, retrieval stores and tools, resource consumption, security events and the versions in force at the time; that this telemetry lands in a central place where it can be searched and correlated end to end; that baselines and anomaly alerts exist; and that retention and the chosen signals are revisited as the system changes. The durable record of agent decisions belongs to MI-21 and spend alerting to MI-9.

requirements.title: AI System Alerting and Denial of Wallet (DoW) / Spend Monitoring
requirements.summary: The organisation can show that money spent on usage-priced AI services is bounded and watched. It can show a hard spending cap at organisation level, budgets that cascade down to departments, projects and keys, alerts at staged thresholds and on unusual spending, automatic throttling or suspension when a hard limit is reached, attribution of every cost to a business unit, project, user or use case, and investigation of each spend alert to tell legitimate use from misconfiguration or a deliberate attempt to run up costs. Request-rate limits for availability are MI-8's subject.

requirements.title: Human Feedback Loop for AI Systems
requirements.summary: An organisation must be able to show that the users and subject-matter experts of each AI system have an easy way to rate outputs, comment on them and report harmful, biased or insecure behaviour; that what is collected is tied to the system's performance indicators, triaged by severity and tracked to an action and an outcome; that participation is watched for decline; and that people who reported something hear what happened where feasible. This is the human channel: operational telemetry belongs to MI-4 and automated model-based grading to MI-15.

requirements.title: Providing Citations and Source Traceability for AI-Generated Information
requirements.summary: An organisation must be able to show that its AI systems which produce informational answers link each claim to the specific passage and version of the source it came from, that users can open or read that source, that content drawn from the model's general knowledge or heavy synthesis is labelled as uncited rather than given an invented reference, that citation relevance and broken or changed links are checked, and that users and technical reviewers are told how citations work and where they fall short. What may enter the knowledge base is governed by MI-2.

requirements.title: Using Large Language Models for Automated Evaluation (LLM-as-a-Judge)
requirements.summary: Where an organisation uses one model to grade another system's outputs, it must be able to show that the judge works from a written rubric with a defined scope and output format; that its agreement with expert human grading was measured on a representative set before its scores were relied on, and is re-measured over time; that sampled outputs are judged on a recorded cadence; and that flagged items, low-confidence verdicts and a sample of passes go to a person with a route for escalation. Pre-release acceptance belongs to MI-5 and general user feedback to MI-11.

requirements.title: Preserving Source Data Access Controls in AI Systems
requirements.summary: An organisation should be able to show that when an AI system, especially one using retrieval augmented generation, ingests documents and records, the permissions those items carried at source travel with them, so a user can only receive answers built from content they could have opened directly. It should be able to show which enforcement pattern each retrieval index uses, that the pattern does not rely on model instructions, and that logging, red teaming and reconciliation catch any path that bypasses it.

requirements.title: Agent Decision Audit and Explainability
requirements.summary: The organisation can show, for each agent use case, a recorded risk analysis choosing how much of the agent's decision-making it keeps, from minimal security logging with human oversight up to a full tamper-evident trail with reasoning and context. It can show that the records it keeps at that depth actually let it reconstruct what an agent did, and where required why, for investigation and accountability, and it states plainly where a model provider's hidden reasoning limits what can be captured. Approval of individual actions is a separate mitigation.

templates.title: Sensitive content is removed or de-identified before knowledge-base data reaches AI embeddings and retrieval
templates.description: Content from internal knowledge sources passes a recorded set of filtering rules before it is embedded or used by a model, and what cannot be safely cleaned is kept in a segregated environment.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Data Protection Officer / AI Platform Lead
templates.objective: To keep personal, proprietary, operational and privileged information out of AI embeddings and retrieval by filtering knowledge-base content before ingestion.
templates.successCriteria:
Every knowledge source feeding an AI pipeline is listed with the sensitive categories it may contain and the business need for ingesting it.
A rule set names the treatment for each sensitive category, with the utility trade-offs recorded.
The ingestion pipeline applies the rules before embedding and logs what each document had applied.
Sources too sensitive to clean are served only from a segregated AI environment with tighter access.
Sampling of filtered content and user reports drive recorded updates to the rules.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the list of knowledge sources ingested by AI pipelines, with the sensitive categories identified in each and the business need.
Obtain the filtering rule set with the treatment per category and its version history.
Obtain the ingestion pipeline configuration and the filtering logs for the period.
Obtain the design and access configuration of any segregated AI environment.
Obtain the register of user reports of exposed content and the latest sampling results.

Analysis:
Compare the source list with what the ingestion jobs actually read to find unlisted sources.
Check that each sensitive category found in the sources has a rule and that the pipeline runs the rules before embedding rather than after.
Sample embedded or indexed content and search it for personal data, credentials, unreleased financial information and privileged material the rules should have caught.
Check that sources marked too sensitive to clean appear only in the segregated environment and that its access list is narrower.
Trace user reports and sampling misses to the rule changes they produced.

Output:
A list of unlisted sources and uncovered categories.
Miss and over-filtering counts from the sample, by category.
A record of rule changes made and any finding still open, with an owner.

title.en: List the knowledge sources feeding AI pipelines and the sensitive categories in each

description.en: Identify every wiki, document management system, database, collaboration site or intranet that AI systems ingest for training, embeddings or retrieval. For each, record the business purpose for including it, and which sensitive categories it may hold: personal data, proprietary business information, internal operational detail such as configurations and credentials, customer financial data, and legal, regulatory or privileged material. Attach the list.

evidenceHint.en: Knowledge source list, one row per source, with the AI use, business need and the sensitive categories it may contain

text.en: List every internal knowledge source an AI pipeline ingests.
Record the AI system and purpose each source serves.
Remove or justify sources the business purpose does not need.
Identify which sensitive categories each source may contain, with examples found.
Date the list and record who compiled it.

title.en: Write the filtering rule set with a treatment for each sensitive category

description.en: For each category on the list, choose how it will be handled before ingestion: masked with a placeholder, redacted, generalised to a broader term, replaced by a token resolvable only in a separate system, or replaced by synthetic data for training. Record where a treatment would remove information the use case needs, and the decision taken, and how context changes sensitivity. Attach the versioned rule set.

evidenceHint.en: Versioned filtering rule set naming each sensitive category, its detection method, its treatment and the recorded utility trade-off

text.en: Write a detection method for each sensitive category, such as patterns or a classifier.
Assign each category one treatment: masking, redaction, generalisation, tokenisation or synthesis.
Note where context changes whether an item is sensitive and how the rule handles it.
Record where a treatment removes information the use case needs, and the decision.
Version the rule set and record who approved each version.

title.en: Configure the ingestion pipeline to apply filtering rules before embedding

description.en: Place the rule set in the ingestion pipeline ahead of chunking, embedding and indexing, and before any call to an external service, so unfiltered content never reaches the vector store or a provider. Log, for each document, the rule version run and the treatments applied, without logging the sensitive values themselves. Attach the configuration and a sample log.

evidenceHint.en: Ingestion pipeline configuration showing the filtering stage before embedding, with a sample per-document filtering log

text.en: Insert the filtering stage before chunking and embedding in each pipeline.
Confirm no pipeline sends content to an external service before filtering.
Load the current rule set version into each pipeline.
Log per document the rule version and the treatments applied.
Check the log omits the sensitive values that were removed.
Run a known test document through and keep the filtered result.

title.en: Move sources too sensitive to sanitise into a segregated AI environment

description.en: Where a source cannot be made safe by filtering, serve it only from a separate AI environment with its own models and vector store, a narrower access list, stronger encryption and restricted network connectivity, scoped to the access domains that need it. Attach the environment design and its access configuration.

evidenceHint.en: Segregated AI environment design with its source list, access list, encryption settings and network restrictions

text.en: Mark the sources the rule set cannot make safe for general use.
Provision a separate vector store and model deployment for those sources.
Restrict the environment's access list to the access domains that need it.
Restrict network connectivity to and from the environment.
Remove those sources from any general-purpose index that still holds them.

title.en: Log and act on reports of sensitive content surfacing from AI knowledge sources

description.en: Give users and reviewers a route to report sensitive information they see in AI answers or retrieved passages, trace each report to the source document and the filtering that let it through, purge the content and update the rules. Track new kinds of sensitive data introduced by new business units or regulations the same way. Attach the report register for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Register of exposure reports for the period with source document, cause, purge confirmation and rule change for each

text.en: Publish the reporting route to users and reviewers of AI answers.
Log each report with the content seen and the source document.
Identify why the filtering rules did not catch the content.
Purge the content from the index and confirm removal.
Raise a rule change for the gap and record its version number.

title.en: Sample filtered knowledge-base content for sensitive data the rules missed

description.en: Draw a sample of processed documents and indexed chunks and search them by hand and with tools for sensitive data that escaped filtering, and for over-filtering that removed information the use case needed. Record misses and false positives by category and the rule changes they prompt. Attach the sampling record.

evidenceHint.en: Sampling record with sample size, misses and false positives by category, and the rule changes raised

text.en: Draw a sample of filtered documents and indexed chunks across sources.
Search the sample for each sensitive category the rule set covers.
Record each miss with the rule that should have caught it.
Record each case where filtering removed information the use case needed.
Raise rule changes for the findings and note their owners.

templates.title: Model inputs and outputs filtered at every trust boundary
templates.description: Each flow into and out of a model carries defined input and output checks, those checks run on live traffic and log every block, redaction or cancellation, and their effectiveness is measured against known attack and leakage samples.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: AI Platform Lead / Application Security Lead
templates.objective: To ensure harmful prompts, sensitive data and abusive or malformed responses are caught wherever data crosses between users, application components and a model.
templates.successCriteria:
Every flow carrying data to or from a model, including content sent out for embedding, is listed with the checks applied to it.
Input checks address injection attempts and sensitive data; output checks address leakage, oversized replies, format deviations and offensive content.
The approach to filtering streamed replies is decided and written down with the exposure it accepts.
Each block, redaction or cancellation is logged with the rule that fired.
A sample set of attacks and leaks is run against the checks and every miss is fixed or recorded as accepted.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the data-flow map of each AI system showing where prompts, responses, inter-component calls and embedding requests cross a trust boundary.
Obtain the input and output check configuration for each boundary, with the rule type behind each check.
Obtain the written decision on how streamed replies are filtered.
Obtain the filter decision log for the period and the latest results of running attack and leakage samples against the checks.

Analysis:
Compare the data-flow map with the deployed architecture and name any boundary that has no check.
Confirm input checks cover injection attempts and sensitive data, and output checks cover leakage, length, format and offensive content.
Confirm content bound for an external embedding service passes a sensitive-data check before it is transmitted.
Sample logged blocks and redactions and trace each one to the rule that produced it.
Compare the sample-run results with the previous run and confirm each miss has a fix or a recorded acceptance.

Output:
A boundary-by-boundary table of checks in place, naming each boundary with none.
A statement of how streamed replies are handled and what exposure that leaves.
A list of sample cases the checks missed, with the fix or acceptance recorded for each.

title.en: Map each data flow into and out of every model and where it is checked

description.en: Draw, for each AI system, every path by which data reaches a model or leaves it: user prompts, responses, calls between application components, retrieval results, and internal content sent to an outside provider to build embeddings. Mark the trust zones each path crosses and the check that sits on it, or that none does. Attach the map with its date and author.

evidenceHint.en: Data-flow map per AI system marking each trust boundary and the input or output check on it

text.en: List the user-facing entry points that pass prompts to each model.
Add calls between application components that carry model input or output.
Add paths where internal content leaves for an outside embedding or model provider.
Mark which trust zone each path starts and ends in.
Name the check on each boundary crossing, or write none where nothing sits there.

title.en: Configure prompt checks for injection attempts and sensitive data

description.en: On every inbound boundary in the map, put a check that flags or blocks injection attempts and abusive input and that removes or masks private data a user includes, especially where the model runs at an outside provider. Use static patterns for well-defined items and a classifier or judge model for subtler cases, and do not rely on system-prompt instructions alone. Attach the configuration showing each rule and its action.

evidenceHint.en: Input check configuration per boundary, listing each rule, its type (pattern or classifier) and its block, mask or flag action

text.en: Add pattern rules for well-defined items such as email addresses and internal code names.
Route prompts through a classifier or judge model trained to spot injection attempts.
Mask or strip private data in prompts bound for an externally hosted model.
Set the action for each rule: block, mask, or allow with a flag.
File the configuration beside the boundary it protects on the data-flow map.

title.en: Configure response checks for leakage, length, format and offensive language

description.en: On every outbound boundary, check model replies before they reach a user or another component: replies far longer than expected, replies that break the expected structure or switch language, signs the model is pushing back against an attack, private data drawn from retrieval or training, offensive wording, and masked values being re-identified. Decide how streamed replies are handled, either held until checked or cancelled mid-stream on detection, and record the exposure that choice leaves. Attach the configuration and the streaming decision.

evidenceHint.en: Output check configuration per boundary and the written streaming decision naming the exposure window accepted

text.en: Set a maximum reply size per use case and record the figure you chose.
Validate structured replies against their expected schema and language.
Detect replies that signal the model is resisting a manipulation attempt.
Scan replies for private data and for masked values that have been re-identified.
Block or rewrite replies containing offensive or inappropriate language.
Write down whether streamed replies are buffered or cancelled on detection, and why.

title.en: Scan internal content for sensitive data before sending it out for embedding

description.en: Where internal documents are sent to an outside service to be converted into embeddings, run a sensitive-data check on the content before transmission, because once stored as vectors it can no longer be inspected or filtered. This task covers the transmission boundary only; deciding which sources may enter a knowledge base belongs to MI-2. Attach the screening configuration and a run log showing items removed.

evidenceHint.en: Pre-embedding screening configuration and a run log showing the items removed or masked before transmission

text.en: Identify each pipeline that sends internal content to an outside embedding service.
Place the sensitive-data check before the transmission step in each pipeline.
Configure the check to remove or mask the data classes you have barred from leaving.
Log the count of items removed or masked on every pipeline run.
Confirm traffic to the outside service is encrypted in transit.

title.en: Triage the period's logged filter blocks, redactions and evasion signals

description.en: Go through the filter decision log for the period: blocks, redactions, cancelled streams, and replies that show the model resisting manipulation. Look for repeated attempts from one source, patterns that suggest a probe of the guardrails, and false blocks that stopped legitimate work, and feed in any user reports of problem replies. Attach the triage record with the actions taken.

evidenceHint.en: Triage record of the period's filter decisions, listing clusters found, false blocks and the rule changes made

text.en: Export the period's blocks, redactions and cancelled streams from the filter log.
Group entries by source and rule to find repeated or coordinated attempts.
Pick out legitimate requests that were blocked and note the rule responsible.
Add user reports of problem replies that no filter caught.
Record each rule change made as a result, with the date applied.

title.en: Run injection, leakage and abuse samples against the filters and record misses

description.en: Keep a set of test inputs covering injection techniques, private data in prompts, prompts that coax oversized or off-format replies, and requests for offensive content. Run it against every boundary's checks, record which cases got through or were wrongly blocked, and compare with the previous run. Attach the results with the fix or acceptance for each miss.

evidenceHint.en: Sample-run results per boundary, listing each case missed or wrongly blocked and its fix or recorded acceptance

text.en: Refresh the sample set with injection techniques seen since the last run.
Run the full sample set against each boundary on the data-flow map.
Record each case that passed through unchecked or was blocked in error.
Compare the miss rate with the previous run and note the change.
Enter a fix or a recorded acceptance against every miss.

templates.title: AI systems released only after passing agreed acceptance criteria
templates.description: Before deployment, each AI system is run against a documented, stakeholder-agreed acceptance plan using representative data, its results and open defects are recorded, and the business owner signs the release with accepted limitations stated.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Business System Owner / AI Engineering Lead
templates.objective: To ensure no AI system reaches production until recorded evidence shows it meets criteria agreed in advance for function, performance, security, fairness, usability and compliance.
templates.successCriteria:
Acceptance criteria for the release were recorded and agreed by the stakeholders the plan names before testing began.
Each criterion states how varied model output is judged and the pass rate the organisation accepts for it.
Every criterion traces to at least one executed test case with its result and evidence.
Defects the organisation classed as critical or high were fixed and re-tested before sign-off.
A signed acceptance record names the approver and lists the limitations and risks accepted.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the acceptance test plan, the acceptance criteria with the record of who agreed them and when, and the description of the test environment and test data.
Obtain the test execution log, the traceability matrix from criteria to test cases, and the evidence attached to each result.
Obtain the defect register for the release and the signed acceptance record.

Analysis:
Confirm the criteria were agreed before the first execution date and that the agreeing parties match those the plan names.
Check the criteria cover function, performance, security and access, fairness, usability, regulatory obligations and error handling, or record why a category does not apply.
Check the test data includes normal, boundary and adversarial cases such as injection attempts and hallucination probes, and demographic variation where fairness is in scope.
Compare the environment's configuration and dependencies with production and list differences.
Trace each criterion to executed cases and compare the measured pass rate with the accepted one.
Confirm critical and high defects were closed with re-test evidence before the sign-off date.

Output:
A criterion-by-criterion table of accepted against measured pass rate.
A list of untested criteria, environment differences, defects open at sign-off and limitations missing from the acceptance record.

title.en: Agree measurable acceptance criteria for the AI system release with business and control stakeholders

description.en: Bring together the business owner, representative users, the AI developers, operations, risk, compliance and information security, and write criteria that can be tested. Because the same prompt can yield differently worded answers, express each criterion as content that must or must not appear and record the pass rate accepted for it. Attach the criteria with the record of agreement.

evidenceHint.en: Acceptance criteria document with an accepted pass rate per criterion and the dated agreement of each named stakeholder

text.en: Name the stakeholders whose agreement the release needs and record them in the plan.
Write criteria for function, performance, security and access, fairness, usability, compliance and error handling.
Express each criterion as content an answer must contain or must exclude rather than an exact match.
Record the pass rate the organisation accepts for each criterion and the reasoning behind it.
Collect each stakeholder's dated agreement before any test is executed.

title.en: Build an acceptance test suite and data set representative of production use

description.en: Set up a test environment configured like production, then assemble cases covering ordinary use, boundary and edge conditions, and failure modes such as prompt injection, hallucination and bias. For a retrieval system, load a test knowledge store with known facts the cases can check answers against. Map every case to the criterion it tests. Attach the suite, the matrix and the environment description.

evidenceHint.en: Acceptance test suite, criterion-to-case traceability matrix and a description of the test environment and data

text.en: Configure the test environment with production's infrastructure, settings and dependencies, and list any difference.
Write cases for ordinary requests, boundary conditions and edge cases.
Add adversarial cases probing injection, fabricated answers and biased outcomes.
Include demographic variation in the data wherever fairness is among the criteria.
Use sanitised or synthetic data where real records cannot be used for testing.
Map each case to the criterion it evidences in the traceability matrix.

title.en: Run the acceptance test plan with end users and record each result

description.en: Run the suite with actual end users or business representatives taking part in executing cases and judging results. Record each outcome with its evidence, calculate the pass rate per criterion, and log every deviation from the expected result as a defect. Attach the execution log.

evidenceHint.en: Test execution log with result, evidence reference and tester per case, plus the pass rate per criterion

text.en: Schedule sessions in which end users or business representatives run and judge cases.
Record pass or fail for each case with the tester's name and date.
Attach screenshots, logs or output files as evidence for every result.
Calculate the measured pass rate for each criterion from the recorded results.
Log each unexpected result as a defect linked to its test case.

title.en: Re-test fixes for acceptance defects classed critical or high

description.en: Give every defect found during acceptance a severity, an owner and a status. For each defect the organisation classes as critical or high, re-run the affected cases after the fix and the full criterion it belongs to, and close it only on passing re-test evidence. Attach the defect register.

evidenceHint.en: Defect register showing severity, owner, fix reference and re-test result for each acceptance defect

text.en: Assign each defect a severity using the organisation's scale and name an owner.
Link each fix to the change or commit that resolved the defect.
Re-run the failed cases and every other case under the same criterion.
Close critical and high defects only when the re-test evidence shows a pass.

title.en: Obtain the business owner's signed acceptance of the AI system release

description.en: Compile the measured pass rates against the accepted ones, the defects still open and the known limitations of the system, and present them to the designated business owner and the other stakeholders the plan names. Their signature approves deployment and records the risks they accept. Attach the signed acceptance record.

evidenceHint.en: Signed acceptance record with measured against accepted pass rates, open defects, accepted limitations and approver names

text.en: Summarise measured against accepted pass rate for every criterion.
List defects still open at the time of sign-off with their severity.
Describe the limitations and residual risks the approvers are asked to accept.
Obtain the dated signature of the business owner and each other stakeholder the plan names.
File the signed record with the release so deployment can be traced to it.

templates.title: Data used by AI systems is classified by sensitivity and checked against defined quality standards
templates.description: Each data source feeding an AI system is registered, labelled under the classification scheme and measured against quality thresholds, and pipelines stop data that fails them.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Head of Data Governance / AI Platform Lead
templates.objective: To make sure data used to build and run AI systems is labelled by sensitivity, fit for its intended purpose, and stopped when it falls short of the standards the organisation sets.
templates.successCriteria:
Every data source used by an AI system is registered with its scope, intended use, known limitations and lineage.
Each registered source carries a sensitivity label from the classification scheme, applied at the source or first ingestion point.
Each source has recorded thresholds for the quality dimensions the organisation chose, and pipeline checks measure them.
Data failing a threshold or exceeding the classification permitted for an environment is held back or alerted on.
A sample audit of labels and quality results found any errors and recorded their correction.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the AI data source register with scope, intended use, limitations, lineage and vetting notes for each source.
Obtain the classification label assigned to each source and the record of any manual validation of automated labels.
Obtain the quality standard listing the dimensions and thresholds set per source.
Obtain the pipeline check configuration and its run results, including blocked loads and alerts.
Obtain the quality issue log and the lineage entries for the transformations applied.
Obtain the latest sample audit of labels and quality results.

Analysis:
Compare the register with the data actually read by AI pipelines and training jobs to find unregistered sources.
Check that each source has a label and that highly sensitive or critical-use sources had their automated labels checked by a person.
Confirm the pipeline checks implement the thresholds recorded in the standard, and that restricted data is refused in environments not cleared for it.
Sample logged quality issues and confirm each was fixed or accepted, with the change recorded in lineage.
Re-perform a handful of labels and quality measurements from the audit sample.

Output:
A list of unregistered, unlabelled or unthresholded sources.
A comparison of recorded thresholds against configured checks.
The label error rate and quality failures found, with their remediation owners.

title.en: Register every AI data source with its scope, intended use, limitations and lineage

description.en: Before a source is used to train, test or run an AI system, vet where it comes from, how reliable it is and what quality controls it already has, then enter it in the register. Record what the data covers, what the AI system uses it for, its known gaps or biases, and the path it takes from origin to the model. Attach the register.

evidenceHint.en: AI data source register, one row per source, with origin, vetting notes, scope, intended use, limitations and lineage

text.en: List the datasets, feeds and repositories each AI system trains on, is tested on or reads at run time.
Record the origin and owner of each source and how reliable it has proved to be.
Describe what each source covers and the AI task it is used for.
Note the known gaps, biases or limits that could make it unfit for that task.
Trace the lineage of each source from origin through transformations to the model.
Mark sources that are new and record the vetting done before first use.

title.en: Label each AI data source with a sensitivity class from the classification scheme

description.en: Apply the organisation's existing classification scheme to every registered source, at the source system where possible or at the first ingestion step otherwise. Automated discovery or classifiers may propose labels, but a person checks them for highly sensitive data and data feeding critical uses such as credit, reporting or customer decisions. Brief the people who label AI data on the scheme. Attach the labelled register and the validation record.

evidenceHint.en: Labelled source register showing each class and how it was assigned, plus the manual validation record and briefing attendance

text.en: Assign a class from the scheme to every source in the register.
Record whether each label came from a tool, from the source system or from a person.
Have a person verify automated labels on highly sensitive or critical-use sources.
Record the handling each class requires inside AI environments, such as permitted uses.
Brief the data stewards and engineers who label AI data and record who attended.

title.en: Set quality dimensions and thresholds for each AI data source

description.en: Decide which quality dimensions matter for each source and the level each must reach, choosing among accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, relevance to the task and how well the data represents the population the model serves. The thresholds are the organisation's own choice; record them with the reasoning. Attach the quality standard.

evidenceHint.en: Quality standard listing, per source, the dimensions measured, the threshold set for each and the rationale

text.en: Pick the quality dimensions that matter for each registered source.
Define how each chosen dimension will be measured on that source.
Set and record the threshold each dimension must meet, with the reason.
Identify the representativeness checks needed to catch bias for the population served.
Date the standard and record who set each threshold.

title.en: Configure pipeline checks that hold back data failing quality or sensitivity rules

description.en: Build validation into the pipelines that feed AI systems so that each load is measured against its thresholds and checked against the classes the destination environment may receive. A load that fails is stopped or raises an alert until remediated, and restricted data is refused in environments such as development sandboxes unless an exception is authorised. Attach the check configuration and sample run output.

evidenceHint.en: Pipeline check configuration per source with sample run output showing passed, alerted and blocked loads

text.en: Add a validation step for each recorded threshold to the pipeline for that source.
Set each check to block the load or raise an alert, and record which.
Record the classes each AI environment is cleared to receive.
Make pipelines refuse data above an environment's cleared class unless an exception is logged.
Add monitoring for shifts in data distribution that could degrade the model.
Run each check against a known-bad sample and keep the output.

title.en: Resolve logged data quality issues and record each fix in the lineage

description.en: Work each quality failure or distribution shift the checks report: cleanse, fill, correct, standardise or deduplicate the data, or accept it with a reason. Record every transformation in the lineage so the dataset the model used can be reconstructed. Attach the issue log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Data quality issue log for the period with the fix or acceptance for each issue and the matching lineage entry

text.en: Log each failed check or distribution alert with its source and date.
Decide whether to correct the data or accept it, and record who decided.
Apply the cleansing or transformation and note the method used.
Add the transformation to the lineage record for the source.
Release the held load only once its checks pass or the acceptance is recorded.

title.en: Audit a sample of sensitivity labels and quality results against the underlying data

description.en: Take a sample of registered sources, re-inspect the data, and judge whether its sensitivity label is right and whether the recorded quality results match what you measure yourself. Record errors and their correction, and feed what you learn into the classifiers, thresholds and briefing. Attach the audit record.

evidenceHint.en: Sample audit record listing sources checked, label and quality findings, error rate and corrections made

text.en: Select the sample, weighting it towards sensitive and critical-use sources.
Inspect the data of each sampled source and decide the class it should carry.
Re-measure the quality dimensions and compare with the pipeline results.
Record each mislabel or quality discrepancy with its correction and owner.
Note any change needed to classifiers, thresholds or the briefing material.

templates.title: AI vendor agreements settle data use, IP, liability and model change terms before use
templates.description: Each AI vendor the organisation relies on operates under a signed agreement that has been assessed against the organisation's own legal, privacy, governance and explainability requirements, and the terms on data handling, intellectual property, responsibilities, service levels and model changes are recorded where the teams using the service can read them.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Head of Procurement / Legal Counsel
templates.objective: To ensure no AI vendor service is used before a signed agreement fixes how data, intellectual property, liability and model changes are handled, and the organisation knows those terms.
templates.successCriteria:
Every external AI model, inference, data or tooling service in use is in a contract register naming its agreement.
A requirements checklist drawn from legal, privacy, AI governance and explainability needs is applied to each agreement before signature.
Per vendor the register records whether prompts and outputs are kept and how long, whether they train models, who receives them and where they are stored.
Per vendor it records IP indemnity, output ownership, lifecycle duties, service levels and model change notice.
No AI service found in use lacks an assessed agreement.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the register of AI vendor agreements, with the service each covers and the data the organisation sends to it.
Obtain the contractual requirements checklist and the record of who contributed to it.
Obtain the completed checklist for each agreement signed or renewed in the period, with the legal sign-off.
Obtain the signed agreements, privacy terms and data processing addenda for a sample of vendors.
Obtain procurement, expense and network egress records showing which external AI services were actually used.

Analysis:
Read the sampled agreements and compare what they say about data persistence, training use, onward sharing, storage location, IP indemnity, output ownership, liability and model change notice with what the register records.
Confirm each signed or renewed agreement has a completed checklist dated before signature, and note requirements marked unmet without a recorded acceptance.
Match the services seen in use against the register to find any used without an assessed agreement.
Compare vendor model change announcements received in the period with the notice commitment the register records for that vendor.

Output:
A vendor-by-vendor table showing which contractual points are settled, which are silent and where the register misstates the agreement.
A list of AI services in use with no agreement or no completed checklist.
A list of unmet requirements accepted at signature, with who accepted each.

title.en: Inventory every external AI service and the agreement that governs it

description.en: List each third party supplying a hosted model, inference API, training or reference data set, or AI development tooling, the business use it serves, what data the organisation sends to it, and the signed documents that bind it: master agreement, privacy terms, data processing addendum, licence. Attach the register with its date and compiler.

evidenceHint.en: Contract register of AI vendors, one row per service, naming the data sent and the governing documents

text.en: Pull AI-related suppliers from procurement records, expense claims and cloud marketplace subscriptions.
Ask each engineering team which hosted models, APIs and data sets their systems call.
Record for every service the business use and the categories of data sent to it.
Attach or link the signed agreement, privacy terms and processing addendum for each row.
Mark any service in use that has no signed agreement and name who is chasing it.

title.en: Compile the requirements an AI vendor agreement must satisfy before signature

description.en: Gather the points the organisation needs every AI vendor agreement to settle: requirements from the legal and privacy functions on data handling and lawful processing, guidance from the AI governance body or ethics committee, explainability needs where outputs affect customers or regulatory reporting, and the testing and tooling expectations for responsible use. Write them as a checklist a reviewer can mark met, unmet or not applicable. Attach the checklist and note who contributed each section.

evidenceHint.en: Contractual requirements checklist for AI vendors, with the contributing function named against each section

text.en: Collect data handling, privacy and lawful processing requirements from the legal and privacy teams.
Add the points the AI governance body or ethics committee wants every supplier to accept.
Add explainability and transparency points for systems whose outputs affect customers.
Add points on responsibilities, liability, service levels, security standards and incident notice.
Add the commitment you need on advance notice of model version changes.
Publish the checklist where procurement and legal reviewers will use it, with its version date.

title.en: Record each AI vendor's commitments on retaining, reusing and sharing the data sent to it

description.en: From the signed terms, extract for every vendor whether prompts, inputs and outputs are logged or kept and for how long, the safeguards applied, whether the data trains or tunes the vendor's models, which other parties receive it, where it is stored and whether jurisdictional storage requirements can be met, and how consent obligations are handled. Where the terms are silent, say so rather than assume. Attach the completed data terms matrix.

evidenceHint.en: Data terms matrix per AI vendor: retention, safeguards, training use, onward sharing, storage location and consent, with clause references

text.en: Note whether the vendor keeps prompts and completions and the period stated in the terms.
Note whether submitted data trains or tunes any vendor model and whether you can opt out.
List the other parties the terms allow the vendor to pass data to.
Record the storage locations offered and whether your residency needs can be met.
Cite the clause behind every entry and mark each point the terms leave unstated.

title.en: Record each AI vendor's terms on training data provenance, IP indemnity and ownership of outputs

description.en: For every vendor supplying a pre-trained model or AI tooling, extract what the agreement discloses about the data used to train the model, whether the vendor indemnifies the organisation against intellectual property claims arising from that training data, who owns outputs and anything built with the vendor's tools, and the licence scope and restrictions. Record the allocation of lifecycle duties, liability limits and warranties alongside. Attach the matrix with clause references.

evidenceHint.en: IP and responsibility matrix per AI vendor: training data disclosure, indemnity, output ownership, licence scope, liability and warranties

text.en: Record what the vendor discloses about the sources and nature of its training data.
Record whether an IP indemnity is offered and any conditions or caps attached to it.
Record who owns generated outputs, fine-tuned models and other derived work.
Record licence scope, use restrictions and dependencies on other licensed components.
Record which party holds each lifecycle duty, the liability limits and any warranties given.

title.en: Assess each new or renewing AI vendor agreement against the requirements checklist before signing

description.en: Before any AI vendor agreement is signed or renewed, a legal reviewer marks each checklist point met, unmet or not applicable against the draft terms, and every unmet point is either negotiated or formally accepted by a named person. The data terms and IP matrices are updated from the final text. Attach the completed checklist, signed off and dated before the signature date.

evidenceHint.en: Completed requirements checklist per agreement, with unmet points, their acceptance or resolution, and sign-off dated before signature

text.en: Route the draft agreement to legal review before any signature is scheduled.
Mark each checklist point met, unmet or not applicable with the clause that decides it.
Negotiate unmet points or record the named person who accepts the gap and why.
Update the vendor's rows in the data terms and IP matrices from the final signed text.
File the dated checklist sign-off with the agreement in the contract register.

title.en: Reconcile AI services in use and vendor change notices against the contract register

description.en: Compare the external AI services actually used in the period, taken from network egress, expense and procurement records, with the contract register, and compare each model change notice received from a vendor with the notice commitment recorded for it. Raise each gap with an owner. Attach the reconciliation and the list of actions.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation of AI services in use and vendor change notices against the register, with each gap, owner and agreed action

text.en: Extract the AI endpoints and suppliers seen in egress logs, expenses and purchase orders.
Match each one to a register row and list those with no assessed agreement.
Compare model change notices received with the notice period each contract promises.
Check that the register still reflects any agreement amended during the period.
Assign an owner and an action to every gap and file the list with the reconciliation.

templates.title: AI services kept available to legitimate users under heavy and abusive load
templates.description: Each exposed AI endpoint has per-use-case keys with request limits, burst throttling and priority tiers, sits behind flood protection and redundant capacity, and is watched for traffic anomalies that are acted on when found.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: IT Operations Lead / AI Platform Lead
templates.objective: To ensure no single user, application or attacker can exhaust AI capacity and deny service or degrade response times for legitimate users and critical workflows.
templates.successCriteria:
Every exposed AI endpoint is listed with the availability and response-time targets the organisation has set for it.
Each use case calls AI services through its own revocable key with a recorded request limit.
Burst throttling, priority tiers, edge flood protection and failover capacity are configured for every listed endpoint.
Traffic anomalies are detected and each one is investigated and acted on.
A load test shows the configured limits hold and critical work keeps priority.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the inventory of exposed AI endpoints with the availability and response-time targets set for each.
Obtain the gateway key register showing one key per use case and the request limit on each.
Obtain the gateway throttling and priority tier configuration, the edge flood protection settings, and the load balancing and failover design.
Obtain the traffic anomaly log for the period with actions taken.
Obtain the most recent load test report.

Analysis:
Compare the endpoint inventory with gateway routes and name endpoints reachable without a gateway key.
Confirm every key has a request limit and that shared keys spanning several use cases do not exist.
Confirm priority tiers place the workflows the organisation calls critical ahead of others.
Sample anomaly log entries and confirm each was investigated and closed with an action.
Read the load test for whether limits held, critical work kept priority and response times met their targets.

Output:
A list of endpoints missing a key, limit, flood protection or failover.
A list of anomalies left uninvestigated.
The load test findings against the targets set, with the fix agreed for each gap.

title.en: Inventory exposed AI endpoints with the availability and response targets set for each

description.en: List every AI model, retrieval or agent endpoint reachable through an API or public interface, who depends on it, and whether it supports a business-critical workflow. Record the availability and response-time targets the organisation has set for each; where none has been set, record that as a gap rather than inventing a figure. Attach the inventory.

evidenceHint.en: Inventory of exposed AI endpoints with dependants, criticality and the availability and response-time targets set for each

text.en: List every AI endpoint exposed through an API or public interface.
Name the applications and user groups that depend on each endpoint.
Mark which endpoints serve workflows the organisation treats as critical.
Enter the availability and response-time targets set for each, or note none set.

title.en: Issue a separate gateway key with a request quota for each AI use case

description.en: Route every consumer of AI services through a central API gateway and give each use case its own key rather than sharing one. Set a request quota on each key, so a misbehaving application can be cut off alone and its consumption attributed. Attach the key register showing owner, use case and quota per key.

evidenceHint.en: Gateway key register, one row per use case, naming owner, endpoint and request quota

text.en: Place each AI endpoint behind the central API gateway.
Replace any key shared across use cases with one key per use case.
Set a per-minute or per-hour request quota on each key and record the value.
Record the owner and use case of each key in the register.
Confirm a single key can be revoked without affecting any other consumer.

title.en: Configure burst throttling, input validation and priority tiers at the AI gateway

description.en: Add dynamic throttling that smooths bursts of requests, validation that turns away malformed or oversized inputs before they reach the model, and service tiers that let the workflows marked critical in the inventory through first when capacity is saturated. Attach the gateway configuration showing each setting.

evidenceHint.en: AI gateway configuration showing burst throttling, input size and format validation, and priority tier assignments

text.en: Enable burst throttling and record the burst allowance chosen per endpoint.
Reject malformed requests and those above the input size you set.
Define the priority tiers and assign each key to one of them.
Place the workflows marked critical in the inventory in the top tier.

title.en: Configure edge flood protection, load balancing and failover for AI inference

description.en: Put network-level DDoS protection in front of exposed AI endpoints, spread inference traffic across instances and zones with dynamic load balancing, provide redundant capacity for failover, and isolate core inference services in their own containers so an overloaded upstream component cannot starve them. Attach the architecture record and the protection settings.

evidenceHint.en: Architecture record and settings for edge DDoS protection, load balancing across zones, failover capacity and inference isolation

text.en: Enable the network DDoS protection service for each exposed AI endpoint.
Configure load balancing of inference traffic across instances and zones.
Provision standby capacity and document how traffic fails over to it.
Run core inference in containers isolated from upstream components.

title.en: Investigate AI traffic anomalies and throttle or revoke the keys responsible

description.en: Watch request volume, latency and error rates for each endpoint in real time, with detection for floods, prompt flooding, repeated costly inference calls and slow low-volume attacks. Investigate each anomaly raised, throttle or revoke the key or source responsible where it is abuse, and log the outcome. Attach the anomaly log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: AI traffic anomaly log for the period with source, finding and action (throttle, revoke or none) for each entry

text.en: Review the real-time dashboard of volume, latency and errors per endpoint.
Open an investigation for each anomaly the detection raises.
Identify the key, user or source address behind each anomaly.
Throttle or revoke the responsible key where the traffic is abusive.
Log the finding and action against each anomaly and close it.

title.en: Test AI endpoints under flood and costly-prompt traffic against their targets

description.en: Simulate high-volume traffic, bursts of complex prompts and repeated expensive calls against a non-production copy of each critical endpoint. Check that request limits and throttling engage, that critical workflows keep priority, that failover works, and that response times stay within the targets in the inventory. Attach the test report with each gap and its agreed fix.

evidenceHint.en: Load test report per critical endpoint comparing limits, priority, failover and response times with the recorded targets

text.en: Script flood, burst and costly-prompt scenarios for each critical endpoint.
Run them against a non-production environment built like production.
Record whether quotas, throttling and priority tiers engaged as configured.
Take one instance or zone down mid-test and record failover behaviour.
Enter each gap against its target with the fix agreed and its owner.

templates.title: Production AI systems run approved, pinned model versions and change only through tested upgrades
templates.description: Every production AI system calls an explicitly chosen model version recorded in an inventory, each output can be traced to the version that produced it, and a new version replaces a pinned one only after evaluation, staged rollout and a tested rollback.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: AI Platform Lead / Model Risk Manager
templates.objective: To ensure AI behaviour in production stays predictable by fixing each model version and adopting newer ones only after they have been evaluated and approved.
templates.successCriteria:
Every production AI system is listed with its pinned model version, the rationale for that choice and a business owner.
Supplier terms cover version selection, release notes, advance notice of new and retired versions, and no forced upgrades.
Each application requests an explicit version and logs it against every output.
Each upgrade has an evaluation against the baseline, a staged rollout and a tested rollback.
Periodic checks find production calls only using approved versions.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the model inventory listing each production system, its pinned version, the reason for that choice and its owner.
Obtain supplier contracts or terms covering versioning, release notes, deprecation notice and version selection.
Obtain the model call configuration of each application and a sample of output logs showing the model version.
Obtain the evaluation, approval and rollout records for each version change in the period, including rollback tests.
Obtain the latest audit of production calls against the inventory.

Analysis:
Compare the inventory with model calls observed in production logs and name any system calling an unlisted or floating version alias.
Read the supplier terms for each of the four commitments and note which are missing.
Trace a sample of outputs to the version recorded in the log and confirm it matches the inventory for that date.
For each version change, confirm an evaluation against the baseline, an approval and a rollback test preceded full rollout.
Check that advisories about pinned versions received in the period were assessed.

Output:
A list of systems not pinned or not matching the inventory.
A list of missing supplier commitments.
A list of version changes made without evaluation, approval or a rollback test.

title.en: Inventory deployed AI models with their pinned version, application and owner

description.en: List every AI model used in production, whether supplied by a vendor or built in-house, with the exact version each application uses, the business owner, why that version was chosen and the results of the validation that cleared it. Attach the inventory; it is the approved baseline the other tasks check against.

evidenceHint.en: Model version inventory, one row per production use, giving exact version, application, owner, selection rationale and validation reference

text.en: List every production application that calls an AI model.
Record the exact model version each one uses, not a floating alias.
Name the business owner of each application and model pairing.
Write the reason that version was chosen and link its validation results.
Record the tooling used to manage and deploy model versions.

title.en: Obtain supplier commitments on model versioning, release notes and deprecation notice

description.en: During procurement or renewal with each external model supplier, secure terms that let you select and stay on a specific version, a clear version numbering scheme, release notes describing changes in behaviour, data and performance, advance notice of new releases and retirement dates, access to test new versions before adopting them, and a channel for reporting regressions. Attach the clauses or written confirmations per supplier.

evidenceHint.en: Per-supplier contract clauses or written confirmations covering version selection, numbering, release notes, deprecation notice, test access and feedback

text.en: Confirm the supplier's API lets you request a specific model version.
Obtain the supplier's version numbering scheme and a sample of its release notes.
Secure advance notice of new versions and of retirement dates for old ones.
Agree that production use is never moved to a new version without your action.
Arrange sandbox or trial access for testing new versions before adoption.
Record the channel and contact for reporting regressions to the supplier.

title.en: Configure each application to request an explicit model version and log it per output

description.en: Change every model call so it names the version in the inventory rather than a latest or default alias, and add the version used to the log entry, and where practical the metadata, of each transaction, decision or output. Attach the configuration for each application and a sample of log lines showing the version.

evidenceHint.en: Model call configuration per application naming the pinned version, and sample output logs carrying the version

text.en: Replace floating version aliases in every model call with the inventory version.
Add the model version field to each output log entry.
Attach the model version to output metadata where the consumer can read it.
Pull sample log lines from each application showing the version recorded.

title.en: Evaluate each candidate model version against the pinned baseline before approval

description.en: When a supplier releases a new version, or a vulnerability or behaviour concern is published about a pinned one, test the candidate on your own use cases and data: performance against the baseline, bias and fairness, new security weaknesses and integration behaviour. Record the decision to adopt, defer or reject it and the reasons. Attach the evaluation and decision record.

evidenceHint.en: Evaluation report for each candidate version comparing it with the baseline, with the adopt, defer or reject decision and reasons

text.en: Log each new release notice or advisory about a version in the inventory.
Run the candidate against the baseline's test set on your own data.
Assess changes in bias, fairness and security exposure from the release notes and tests.
Run integration tests with every application that would adopt the version.
Record the adopt, defer or reject decision, its reasons and who made it.

title.en: Deploy approved model versions in stages with a rehearsed rollback

description.en: Introduce an approved version through a canary or blue/green deployment, watch its behaviour against the baseline during the rollout, and rehearse reverting to the previously pinned version before full cutover. Update the inventory once the rollout completes. Attach the rollout record and the rollback test result.

evidenceHint.en: Rollout record for each version change showing stages, observed behaviour, rollback rehearsal result and the updated inventory row

text.en: Deploy the approved version to a canary slice or parallel environment first.
Compare its live behaviour with the previous version during the rollout.
Rehearse switching back to the previously pinned version and time it.
Complete the cutover and update the version in the inventory.

title.en: Audit production model calls against the approved version inventory

description.en: Periodically extract the model versions actually called in production from the output logs and compare them with the inventory, looking for floating aliases, unapproved versions and versions the supplier has announced for retirement. Attach the audit result with each mismatch and its fix.

evidenceHint.en: Audit comparing logged production model versions with the inventory, listing each mismatch or upcoming retirement and its fix

text.en: Extract the distinct model versions called in production from the logs.
Match each to its inventory row and flag any version without approval.
Flag pinned versions the supplier has scheduled for retirement.
Record the fix and owner for each mismatch found.

templates.title: Access to AI data is granted by defined role, on least privilege, and recertified
templates.description: People and non-human identities reach AI training, inference and model data only through roles in an approved matrix, enforced at every layer, logged, and recertified by data owners.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: CISO / Data Owner
templates.objective: To restrict access to the data AI systems are built and run on to the roles and machine identities that need it, and to keep that access logged and periodically confirmed.
templates.successCriteria:
Every human role and non-human identity touching AI data is listed with its access needs per lifecycle stage.
An access control matrix maps each role to data classes and permitted actions, with incompatible duties identified and separated.
Stores, ML platforms, APIs and applications holding AI data enforce the matrix, with no grant outside it.
People use multi-factor authentication and non-human identities use managed, rotated credentials.
Access is logged, and the last recertification removed every grant its owner did not confirm.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the inventory of roles and non-human identities with their documented access needs.
Obtain the access control matrix and the record of segregation-of-duties conflicts.
Obtain permission exports from each AI data store, ML platform, API gateway and consuming application.
Obtain authentication configuration for people and the credential register for non-human identities.
Obtain the access log configuration, the log review records and the latest recertification results.

Analysis:
Compare each permission export with the matrix and list grants the matrix does not support, including broad or default grants.
Check that no single role holds a combination of duties the conflict record says must be split.
Confirm every human account requires multi-factor authentication and every machine credential is held in managed storage and rotated on the schedule set.
Sample access log entries and confirm each records identity, data, action and time, and that denied attempts appear.
Compare the recertification decisions with the current exports to confirm revocations were carried out, including for leavers and role changes.

Output:
A list of excess or unmatched grants by layer.
A list of duty conflicts and authentication gaps.
The recertification completion figure and any revocation not carried out.

title.en: Inventory the human roles and non-human identities that access AI data

description.en: List every job role and every model, MLOps pipeline, automation script and service account that reads or writes data used by or produced from AI systems. For each, record the actions it needs on which data at each lifecycle stage: collection, annotation, training, validation, inference and monitoring. Attach the inventory.

evidenceHint.en: Inventory of roles and non-human identities, one row each, with the data and actions needed per lifecycle stage

text.en: List the human roles that work with AI data, such as data scientists, data stewards and auditors.
List the models, pipelines, scripts and service accounts that touch AI data.
Record the data assets each one needs, including datasets, model artefacts and configuration.
Note the actions each needs on each asset: read, write, modify, delete or execute.
Mark the lifecycle stage in which each access need arises.

title.en: Build the access control matrix mapping AI roles to data classes and actions
